newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Pilgrims pack Fatima to mark 80th anniversary.
newsitem.headline: Pilgrims pack Fatima to mark 80th anniversary.

text.p: Thousands of pilgrims, many on foot and some even shuffling along on their knees, converged on the Catholic shrine of Fatima on Monday for the 80th anniversary of the "apparition" of the Virgin Mary to three Portuguese shepherd children.

The shrine, one of the world's most hallowed sites for Roman Catholics, marks the spot where the Virgin is believed to have appeared to the children at midday on May 13, 1917, and again for the next five months.

Officials expected up to 400,000 people, slightly more than usual, to pack the square outside the sanctuary on Tuesday for a series of masses that each year draw the faithful from as far afield as eastern Europe, Japan and the United States.
While most pilgrims arrive by bus or car, thousands make the entire trip on foot, often taking days to get there, either to fulfil a promise or as a sign of particular devotion.
One group of 12 had set out on foot from the small town of Agueda, south of Oporto, to make the three-day trek of more than 60 miles (100 km) to Fatima.
Among them was 70-year-old Maria do Carmo who said she had made the trip every year for 25 years -- ever since her son returned safely from Portugal's colonial wars in Africa.
Some pilgrims cover the final kilometre or so on their knees along a special pathway.

"I made a promise after my daughter recovered from a head injury," said one woman, who gave her name as Giselda. She was inching her way along the pathway on her knees with her daughter, now four, perched on her shoulders.
Among leading church figures expected at Fatima, some 80 miles (130 km) north of Lisbon, was the 1996 Nobel Peace laureate Carlos Ximenes Belo.

Belo, bishop of Dili, capital of the former Portuguese Pacific colony of East Timor, told journalists on his arrival in Lisbon that he was going "to give thanks to the Virgin" and pray for peace in the troubled territory which has been occupied by Indonesia since 1976.
One notable absentee will be the sole survivor of the child visionaries who said they heard the Virgin deliver three prophecies about the state of the world, only two of which were ever disclosed.
According to the writings of Sister Lucia, the Virgin Mary predicted the end of the First World War and the fall of Communism in eastern Europe.
But the third prophecy was never made public, stirring speculation that it alluded to some future catastrophe.

However, Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, head of the Vatican's Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith and number three in the Church hierachy, said last year that the so-called 'Third Secret of Fatima' contained nothing alarming.
He added that he did not know whether the papacy, which was informed of it in 1957, would eventually reveal its contents.
Sister Lucia de Jesus dos Santos, who recently celebrated her 90th birthday, hardly ever leaves the Carmelite convent in central Portugal which she entered in 1929.
Two exceptions were for papal visits to the shrine in 1982 and 1991, when Pope John Paul, noted for his devotion to the Virgin, came to give thanks for surviving an assassination attempt.
The Pope was shot and wounded by Turkish gunman Ali Agca in Rome on May 13, 1981, and attributes his survival to divine intervention by the Virgin of Fatima.
"The only times sister Lucia has left have been to go to the doctor, to meet the Pope and to vote. She has never failed to exercise her right to vote," her mother superior told Reuters recently.
